title: North Fork: Colonial Claims and Continuing Native Rights
summary: Southold’s English officials used confirming deeds and a colonial patent to consolidate claims across the North Fork. Native signers, reserved rights and later objections show a process of dispossession, not one uncontested sale.

history_title: Confirming deeds, a patent and continuing Native rights
history_content:
A homeland larger than one town center

The North Fork is the long peninsula between Long Island Sound and Peconic Bay, running east from the Wading River and Riverhead area through Mattituck, Cutchogue, Southold and Orient. Its Native history cannot be represented by a single pin in Southold hamlet. Names such as Pauquaconsuk, Corchaug and Mattatuck appear within the colonial documents themselves. Those records describe an inhabited landscape of land, waterways, hunting and fishing interests—not an empty peninsula waiting to become a town. Southold Town Records, volume II, pp. 6–10

Who sought a permanent colonial claim?

On December 7, 1665, a written confirmation named Captain John Yongs, Barnabas Horton and Thomas Maps as recipients acting for Southold's inhabitants. These were representatives of an English settler town. The document asserted that earlier transactions had already acquired land from Native predecessors, acknowledged forty yards of trading cloth or its equivalent, and sought to confirm the claim for the town's inhabitants and their heirs. Ambuscow, Pammatuks, Tauckequon, Nowunneg and many other Native people are named with marks in the recorded copy. Their presence matters: the town was seeking Native confirmation, not dealing with a people who had disappeared. Southold Town Records, volume II, pp. 6–8

The confirmation describes a wide landscape from Wading Creek, called Pauquaconsuk, toward Plum Island, with the Sound to the north. Its southern description reaches the bay and disputed meadow country near Red Creek, called Toyonge. It combines earlier bargains and claims in one written instrument. It should not be read as evidence that every acre first changed hands on that day or that every family understood its implications in the same way. Southold Town Records, volume II, pp. 6–8

What an English patent added

On October 31, 1676, Edmund Andros, governing New York for James, Duke of York and Albany, issued a patent to Southold's named officials and associates. The recipients included Isaac Arnold, John Yong, Joshua Horton, Barnabas Horton, Benjamin Yongs, Samuel Glover and Jacob Corey. The patent described rights to woods, meadows, water and other resources, and made the town's tenure answerable to an English legal model—the manor of East Greenwich in Kent—with an annual payment to the Duke. This was colonial government translating a Native homeland into an inheritable estate and a jurisdiction it claimed authority to regulate. Southold Town Records, volume II, pp. 8–11

Yet the same patent expressly contemplated land within its broad limits that had not been purchased from Native people. It said such land could be purchased according to law. That clause is essential: a colonial grant of town government was not itself proof that all Native title had already been acquired. The patent also qualified its southern boundary by the agreement following Southampton and Southold's court dispute. Southold Town Records, volume II, pp. 9–10

Boundaries, testimony and contested authority

At the November 1667 trial between the two settler towns, Richard Woodhull reported that Native leaders had refused to sell southern land because it belonged to Shinnecock people. Native witnesses appeared and said part of the payment was still owed. The jury initially favored Southampton; Southold appealed, and the court temporarily divided meadow use between them. A colonial courtroom was deciding whose papers and claims would prevail, while Native testimony recorded rights and obligations that a simple sale label obscures. Read the fuller account at Aquebogue and in the western Southampton chapter. Documents Relative to the Colonial History of New York, volume XIV, pp. 600–602

Land was not only a piece of paper

These records show Native territorial authority, continued use and obligations; they do not support saying Native people had no concept of land rights. The difference lay in the kinds of rights asserted and in who gained power to interpret and enforce them. The Ocquebauck agreement, as quoted by Tooker, reserved planting land for Native parties during their lives. A limited lifetime provision could be used within a colonial property system even though a homeland's significance extended across generations. Documents Relative to the Colonial History of New York, volume XIV, pp. 600–602; Indian Place-Names on Long Island and Islands Adjacent, pp. 25

Later community objections and petitions must remain part of the story. The existence of a confirming deed or patent does not establish consent to every later restriction, the end of Native belonging, or the disappearance of descendants. Explore Yennecock / Southold Town for the continuing struggle over access, and Corchaug Ancestral Land for the broader homeland context. Amanhansuck or Corchaug: The History of Southold’s Original People

Continue with Aquebogue, Western Southampton, Yennecock / Southold Town and Corchaug Ancestral Land.
whereintheworld_content: The shaded area shows the North Fork mainland as regional context, using today's Riverhead and Southold shorelines and municipal edges for orientation. It is not a recovered survey of the 1665 confirmation or 1676 patent. Their older western line and contested southern meadows differ from modern town boundaries. Detached islands, including Plum Island named in the documents, are not included in this mainland shape. The western Southampton layer presents the southern dispute separately. A modern shoreline also cannot recover the exact seventeenth-century coast. Southold Town Records, volume II, pp. 6–14; NYS Civil Boundaries: Towns
